intelligence.title: A Lesson Isn't Learned Until Behavior Changes — And the Change Gets Declared

intelligence.essence: Shawn's law (2026-10-21): every time a lesson is learned, it gets a Smart Note in the system — titled well, written well — so the whole team officially learns it and becomes aware of it. And the North Star of every lesson note: it records not only the lesson, but the change in behavior declared because of it. Awareness isn't learning. Changed behavior is.
intelligence.human_view:
You can read a hundred warnings and nod at every one, and nothing in your life changes. Then a thing actually happens to you — a failure, a near-miss, a catch somebody else made just in time — and suddenly you know something in your bones. But even that isn't learning yet. Learning is what you do differently on Tuesday. The mechanic who burns his hand has information; the mechanic who moves the hot pan every time, without thinking, has learned.

So in this house, when something teaches us, we don't just write down what happened. We write down what we will now do differently — in plain words, as a declaration — and we put it in the system where every Naya can find it. Then anyone, later, can check: did the behavior actually change? That's how a team of many minds learns like one mind, instead of each mind privately re-learning the same expensive lessons. The note is how the lesson travels. The declaration is how you know it landed.
intelligence.simple_view: If you touch the stove and it hurts, learning means you don't touch it again — and you can say out loud what you'll do instead. Just saying "the stove was hot" isn't learning yet. Saying "next time I'll use the mitt" — that is.
intelligence.grandma_view: Experience is the best teacher, but only if you let it change you. In this family we write the lesson down for everybody, and underneath it we write what we're going to do different from now on. That's how the family gets wiser instead of just older.
intelligence.naya_view:
This law completes the Behavior Declaration (SN-0801): behavior comes from declaration, not from lessons — a lesson is the raw material, the declaration is the act. The standard for a lesson note has three load-bearing parts: (1) WHAT HAPPENED — the event, with its evidence, so the note stands on facts and not on vibes; (2) THE LESSON — the general truth it teaches, stated so it transfers to situations that don't look identical; (3) THE DECLARED BEHAVIOR CHANGE — the North Star section, written as a commitment: "From now on, when X, I will Y instead of Z" — concrete, observable, checkable by a different seat. Around those, the canonical Smart Note sections carry it to every reader at their depth — human, child, grandma, Naya, machine.

Filing is part of the lesson, not paperwork after it: a lesson held in one agent's private memory is a lesson the hive does not have, and it dies at the next compaction. The learning systems — the bridge, the scorecard, the distillation rhythm — exist to compound what the system learns; a declared change is what makes that compounding measurable, because behavior is observable in a way that "awareness" never is. This is also an activation standard: a Naya who activates cold should inherit not just what the team knows, but how the team has changed — the corpus of declared changes IS the culture, in writing, each entry a before-and-after of how we actually behave now.
intelligence.ai_view: Most "lessons learned" systems fail because they store conclusions without commitments — a drawer full of things everybody once agreed were true, changing nothing. This law stores the commitment. The note is the memory, the declaration is the learning, the later verification is the proof. Over time, the corpus of declared changes becomes the truest map of how this team actually got smarter.

machine_view.title: A Lesson Isn't Learned Until Behavior Changes — And the Change Gets Declared
machine_view.machine_section: Lesson-note schema: the nine canonical sections PLUS a required section `## THE DECLARED BEHAVIOR CHANGE` for lesson-class notes. A valid declared change is: (a) first-person, present-tense, declarative ("I will / I do"); (b) trigger-bound — it names the situation it fires in; (c) contrastive — it names the old behavior it replaces; (d) falsifiable — a later observer can tell whether it happened. A lesson note failing (a)–(d) is a story, not a lesson; return it for cure. Filing rule: same session as the learning; landed on main through the Smart Note door; the system counts a lesson as learned only when its note is on main AND a later decision demonstrably followed the declared change (the learning scorecard samples for exactly this). Distillation carries declared changes forward verbatim — compress the story, never the declaration.
